facts.text: Every human inhabitant of the Tsardom of Moscavia was transformed into an owl-folk on a single night in the spring of the year 994.
No one outside Moscavia was affected; the change stopped precisely at the borders of the Tsardom.
They retain a humanoid shape but bear large, round facial discs like owls, with forward-facing eyes set wide apart on their heads.
Their ears are asymmetrically placed—one higher than the other—giving them exceptional directional hearing.
They possess tufted feathers along their forearms and the back of their necks, with plumage coloration ranging from soft greys and browns to pale creams and rare silvers.
Their fingers are slightly elongated and tipped with small, retractable talons instead of nails.
They cannot fly, but they move with a quiet, gliding gait and have excellent night vision.
They are strongly nocturnal; they feel most alert and comfortable during darkness and tend to drowse or become sluggish in bright daylight.
They have a deep instinct to orient themselves toward sound, turning their heads in sharp, precise rotations to locate noise sources.
Plumage coloration and ear-tuft size vary widely among individuals, and some rare individuals are born with mottled or speckled patterns.
Their talon size and ear asymmetry differ from person to person, much as fingerprints differ among humans.
Six years after the transformation, in the year 1000, the Owl-folk have fully adapted to their new natures and have rebuilt their society accordingly.

preview.summary: The Church of the Veil is a monotheistic faith centered on the Goddess Veil, who performed the divine act known as the Transformation to elevate humanity into a higher form of being. Followers seek to honor her gift by living in accordance with divine will and striving toward spiritual perfection.

timeline.text: The Transformation occurred, an event in which the Goddess Veil reshaped human souls to carry divine potential.
The first temples were established on the Isle of Mists, marking the birth of the Church.
The Doctrine of the Veil was codified into sacred texts known as the Unveiling.
The Great Synod unified the Church under a single hierarchical structure, ending centuries of regional schism.

items.text: The Doctrine of the Veil: Humanity was transformed by the Goddess to carry divine potential within each soul.
All souls are equal before the Veil, and no mortal may claim dominion over another.

items.name: The Three Pillars
items.text: Purity of intention, service to others, and devotion to the Veil form the foundation of righteous living.

timeline.text: The Transformation occurred, an event in which the Goddess Veil reshaped human souls to carry divine potential.
The first temples were established on the Isle of Mists, marking the birth of the Church.
The Doctrine of the Veil was codified into sacred texts known as the Unveiling.
The Great Synod unified the Church under a single hierarchical structure, ending centuries of regional schism.

items.text: The Doctrine of the Veil: Humanity was transformed by the Goddess to carry divine potential within each soul.
All souls are equal before the Veil, and no mortal may claim dominion over another.

items.name: The Three Pillars

preview.name: Tsardom of Moscavia
preview.summary: The Tsardom of Moscavia is a northern realm whose entire human population was transformed into Owlfolk on a single spring night in 994, making it the only nation of feathered humanoids in the known world. It is ruled by a Tsar and governed through a rigid ecclesiastical hierarchy tied to its state church, the Orthodox Church of the Eastern Star.

timeline.text: Every human in Moscavia was transformed into an Owlfolk during the Night of the Great Change, an event of unknown origin that left no explanation and no survivors of the old form.
The Orthodox Church of the Eastern Star declared the transformation divine will and consolidated control over spiritual and civic life, filling the power vacuum left by the old nobility.
Tsar Dmitri II was crowned as the first ruler to govern the transformed nation, establishing a theocratic military state centered on nighttime governance and owl-honoring traditions.
Moscavia closed its borders to all foreign travelers after a delegation from the neighboring Kingdom of Astenmark was found dead at the border, pecked to death by territorial border-owls.

items.name: Velikigrad
items.text: The capital city, built around a massive stone keep that was once a human fortress, now serves as the seat of the Tsar and the Patriarch of the Orthodox Church.

items.name: The Ashenmoor
items.text: A vast peat bog in the southwest that the Owlfolk consider sacred, believed to be where the transformation began.

items.name: The Bone Church of Kholm
items.text: A rural chapel built from the bones of the old human settlers, serving as a pilgrimage site for the faithful.

items.name: The Vigil of the Eastern Star
items.text: The chief annual ceremony held at dawn on the spring equinox, commemorating the Night of the Great Change with song and feather-offerings.
Owlfolk sleep in communal roosts during daylight hours, as direct sunlight causes disorientation and nausea in most transformed citizens.

items.name: The Talon Oath
items.text: Military recruits swear the Talon Oath, binding them to serve until death or until their talons fall out—a condition that has never been documented.

items.name: The Doctrine of the Chosen Feathers
items.text: The Church teaches that the Owlfolk were divinely reshaped to become guardians of the night and that their transformation was a reward for ancient piety.
The Church forbids any inquiry into the cause of the transformation, deeming it blasphemy against the Eastern Star.

items.name: The Law of the Closed Eye
items.text: Any citizen caught spying on Church rituals is subjected to blinding with a hot iron, as the Owlfolk's great eyes are considered the gift of God.
The Church maintains a single library in Velikigrad, containing only religious texts and pre-transformation records deemed compatible with Church doctrine.

items.name: Owling
items.text: The study of owl behavior and anatomy is mandatory for all citizens, taught from childhood as both science and devotion.
No university or academy exists; learning is conducted entirely through Church-affiliated scriptoriums.

items.name: The Tsar
items.text: The supreme ruler, both political and military leader, chosen from the bloodline of the old Moscavian dynasty and crowned by the Patriarch.

items.name: The Patriarch of the Eastern Star
items.text: The head of the Orthodox Church, second only to the Tsar in authority, who oversees all spiritual matters and appoints bishops across the realm.

items.name: The Night Council
items.text: An advisory body of twelve senior owls who meet only after sundown to deliberate on matters of state, law, and Church policy.

facts.text: The Tsardom of Moscavia is a northern realm whose entire human population was transformed into Owlfolk on a single spring night in 994, making it the only nation of feathered humanoids in the known world. It is ruled by a Tsar and governed through a rigid ecclesiastical hierarchy tied to its state church, the Orthodox Church of the Eastern Star.
No university or academy exists; learning is conducted entirely through Church-affiliated scriptoriums.
The Church maintains a single library in Velikigrad, containing only religious texts and pre-transformation records deemed compatible with Church doctrine.
Owlfolk sleep in communal roosts during daylight hours, as direct sunlight causes disorientation and nausea in most transformed citizens.
The Church forbids any inquiry into the cause of the transformation, deeming it blasphemy against the Eastern Star.
Every human in Moscavia was transformed into an Owlfolk during the Night of the Great Change, an event of unknown origin that left no explanation and no survivors of the old form.
The Orthodox Church of the Eastern Star declared the transformation divine will and consolidated control over spiritual and civic life, filling the power vacuum left by the old nobility.
Tsar Dmitri II was crowned as the first ruler to govern the transformed nation, establishing a theocratic military state centered on nighttime governance and owl-honoring traditions.
Moscavia closed its borders to all foreign travelers after a delegation from the neighboring Kingdom of Astenmark was found dead at the border, pecked to death by territorial border-owls.

repeat_of.text: The Tsardom of Moscavia is a northern realm whose entire human population was transformed into Owlfolk on a single spring night in 994, making it the only nation of feathered humanoids in the known world. It is ruled by a Tsar and governed through a rigid ecclesiastical hierarchy tied to its state church, the Orthodox Church of the Eastern Star.

facts.text: The doctrine holds that the Eastern Star — the same divine light that guided the Great Change — also anointed the Tsardom's first ruler, Dmitri II, as God's chosen vessel for temporal governance.

Every Tsar is crowned in the Grand Cathedral of Velikigrad by the Patriarch, who anoints the sovereign with sacred oils blessed under the light of the Eastern Star, making the coronation both a political and a spiritual act.

The Church teaches that resistance to the Tsar's authority is resistance to God's will, and such resistance is classified among the gravest of sins — comparable in severity to blaspheming the transformation itself.

No secular law may be enacted in Moscavia without the tacit approval of the Patriarch and the Synod of Bishops, ensuring that the Church's spiritual authority and the Tsar's temporal authority are inseparable.
The doctrine is codified in the Codex Lucis Orientalis, which devotes an entire section to the sacred covenant between throne and altar, describing the Tsar as 'the Earthly Eye of the Eastern Star.'
Priests are instructed to pray for the Tsar's health and wisdom at every Night Vigil, and failure to do so is grounds for ecclesiastical censure.
The doctrine does not permit the concept of a just rebellion: even a tyrannical Tsar remains divinely appointed, and his subjects' duty is to endure and pray for his reform, not to rise against him.

Bishops and the Patriarch serve at the Tsar's pleasure, but the Church maintains that this arrangement is itself a reflection of divine order — the Tsar governs the body, the Church governs the soul, and both are subject to the same divine light.

The doctrine has never been formally challenged in any Synod proceeding or ecclesiastical record since its codification, though private dissent among monks and parish priests is rumored in certain frontier roosts.
Foreign ambassadors who visit Velikigrad are required to present their credentials not only to the Tsar but also to the Patriarch, acknowledging the dual sovereignty of crown and Church.

facts.text: The Tsardom of Moscavia is a northern realm whose entire human population was transformed into Owlfolk on a single spring night in 994, making it the only nation of feathered humanoids in the known world. It is ruled by a Tsar and governed through a rigid ecclesiastical hierarchy tied to its state church, the Orthodox Church of the Eastern Star.
No university or academy exists; learning is conducted entirely through Church-affiliated scriptoriums.
The Church maintains a single library in Velikigrad, containing only religious texts and pre-transformation records deemed compatible with Church doctrine.
Owlfolk sleep in communal roosts during daylight hours, as direct sunlight causes disorientation and nausea in most transformed citizens.
The Church forbids any inquiry into the cause of the transformation, deeming it blasphemy against the Eastern Star.
The Talon Oath is one of the defining military rites of the Tsardom, administered to every recruit and considered sacred under both military law and Church doctrine.
Every human in Moscavia was transformed into an Owlfolk during the Night of the Great Change, an event of unknown origin that left no explanation and no survivors of the old form.
The Orthodox Church of the Eastern Star declared the transformation divine will and consolidated control over spiritual and civic life, filling the power vacuum left by the old nobility.
Tsar Dmitri II was crowned as the first ruler to govern the transformed nation, establishing a theocratic military state centered on nighttime governance and owl-honoring traditions.
Moscavia closed its borders to all foreign travelers after a delegation from the neighboring Kingdom of Astenmark was found dead at the border, pecked to death by territorial border-owls.

entry_timeline.text: The entire human population of Moscavia was transformed into Owlfolk in a single night, an event the Church would later declare divine will.
The Orthodox Church of the Eastern Star declared the transformation divine will and consolidated control over spiritual and civic life, filling the power vacuum left by the old nobility.
The oath is one of the few military rites that predates Tsar Dmitri II's full codification of the military, having been informally practiced by early border patrols in 995 and 996.
Tsar Dmitri II was crowned as the first ruler to govern the transformed nation, establishing a theocratic military state centered on nighttime governance and owl-honoring traditions.

The Orthodox Church of the Eastern Star teaches that the Tsar of Moscavia rules by direct divine will, not by the consent of the governed or the authority of any earthly institution other than God Himself.

The Church teaches that resistance to the Tsar's authority is resistance to God's will, and such resistance is classified among the gravest of sins — comparable in severity to blaspheming the transformation itself.
Priests are instructed to pray for the Tsar's health and wisdom at every Night Vigil, and failure to do so is grounds for ecclesiastical censure.

Bishops and the Patriarch serve at the Tsar's pleasure, but the Church maintains that this arrangement is itself a reflection of divine order — the Tsar governs the body, the Church governs the soul, and both are subject to the same divine light.
The First Ecclesiastical Council convened in Velikigrad to codify doctrine, declare inquiry into the transformation blasphemous, and close Moscavia's borders.
Moscavia closed its borders to all foreign travelers after a delegation from the neighboring Kingdom of Astenmark was found dead at the border, pecked to death by territorial border-owls.

No secular law may be enacted in Moscavia without the tacit approval of the Patriarch and the Synod of Bishops, ensuring that the Church's spiritual authority and the Tsar's temporal authority are inseparable.
The doctrine is codified in the Codex Lucis Orientalis, which devotes an entire section to the sacred covenant between throne and altar, describing the Tsar as 'the Earthly Eye of the Eastern Star.'
Foreign ambassadors who visit Velikigrad are required to present their credentials not only to the Tsar but also to the Patriarch, acknowledging the dual sovereignty of crown and Church.

Its drawers. A field starts with these (type: title):

- knowledge: what is known or studied, and its frontier

Reply with only one JSON object, shaped exactly like this example:
{"name": "...", "summary": "Two sentences.", "aka": [{"name": "...", "tag": "common", "everyday": true}], "timeline": [{"year": YEAR, "text": "What happened, in one short sentence."}], "drawers": [{"type": "beliefs", "title": "..."}, {"type": "practices", "title": "..."}], "items": [{"drawer": "the drawer's title", "name": "...", "text": "One short sentence.", "kind": "lore"}, {"drawer": "the drawer's title", "text": "A plain statement, in one short sentence."}], "names": [{"name": "...", "kind": "place", "aka": []}]}

- "summary": two sentences: what it is, whose it is, and what it stands for.
- "timeline": 2 to 4 moments in its history, oldest first, each {"year", "text"}: something that happened in that year, never how things stand now. "year" is a year of this calendar, as a bare number no later than 1000; "YEAR" in the example stands for that number.
- "drawers": its drawer outline. Start from the drawers above: keep each that fits, give it a title that suits this field, and drop any it doesn't need; add a drawer of another type only if it clearly needs one. "type" is one of: places, practices, beliefs, knowledge, structure. Don't write people, a timeline or branches as drawers: the app keeps those.

When the item is a thing of its own that could get its own entry (a rite, an office, a council, a doctrine, a text, a site), "name" is its proper name, such as "the Dawn Vigil", and "kind" is lore, place (a site), item (an object) or event. For a plain statement ("Priests may not marry."), give only "drawer" and "text". "text" is one short sentence, under 20 words.

"tag" is "proper" for another formal name, or "common" for what people in the world actually call it day to day. Set "everyday" true on the one common name people use most, false on the rest. An empty list is fine.

Each is {"name", "kind", "aka"}: "name" in full, as you wrote it; "kind" one of character, place, species, race, sphere, event, item, lore; "aka" any other names you used for the same thing. Keep every text to one sentence. No commentary, no markdown fences, just the JSON object.

steps.prompt: Deep Etching: Runes carved into metal using acid-bathed chisels that burn the symbol into the grain. Part of Runeweaving, under Techniques.

facts.text: Deep Etching is the practice of inscribing rune symbols into metal surfaces by first bathing a chisel in corrosive acid, then pressing and dragging it across the metal in a controlled stroke.
The acid eats into the metal's grain, leaving the carved rune permanently embedded as a physical feature of the surface, not merely a marking on top of it.
Unlike engraving or stamping, Deep Etching transforms the metal at a molecular level, bonding the rune's resonant frequencies into the material's dormant song.
The acid used varies by region: Ashenmount Academy weavers traditionally favor a distilled solution of mountain celandine, while coastal workshops use black Coralvine extract.
A Deep Etched rune is considered more durable than one carved by other means, because the acid creates micro-channels that channel ambient Resonance directly into the symbol.
Apprentice weavers typically spend their second year learning Deep Etching before progressing to more advanced techniques like Barkweaving or glass-singing.
The technique requires a steady hand and precise pressure, as too much force can crack the metal and too little leaves a rune too shallow to hold resonance.
Deep Etching is one of the oldest documented techniques in Runeweaving, with early examples found on the boundary stones of the original Ashenmount settlements dating to around the 5th century.
The Valdenmark Ruins contain Deep Etched panels that survived the burning of 602, demonstrating the technique's remarkable permanence even under extreme heat.
Master Weavers can Deep Etch runes onto moving metal objects — such as blades or armor in active use — by synchronizing their carving stroke with the object's rhythm of motion.
The Third Tenet of Runeweaving is particularly relevant to Deep Etching, as the acid solutions and chisel designs used in the technique are considered freely shareable craft knowledge.

elsewhere.text: Deep Etching is one of the foundational techniques taught to Apprentice weavers during their formative years at institutions like Ashenmount Academy.
Deep Etching is a core curriculum subject at the Academy, with dedicated workshops where apprentices practice on scrap iron before moving to precious metals.
Apprentice weavers must demonstrate proficiency in Deep Etching before they are permitted to advance to intermediate techniques such as Barkweaving.
Among a Master Weaver's distinguished skills is the ability to perform Deep Etching on moving metal targets, a feat that requires intimate mastery of Resonance and physical control.

Surviving Deep Etched panels within the ruins are studied by Academy scholars as examples of the technique's extraordinary longevity, some still holding faint resonance nearly four centuries after their creation.
The Third Tenet's emphasis on free knowledge sharing extends to Deep Etching formulas, which regional workshops exchange openly during annual gatherings at the Keldara Runestone.

Faculty housing is built into the cliff face north of the campus, with heated stonework that demonstrates the practical Runeweaving skills of the Academy's own graduates.

steps.prompt: A young runeweaver is summoned at The Border Roosts, where a priest of Orthodox Church of the Eastern Star questions her about Divine Right of the Tsar

local.name: Father Isidor Vekhov
facts: A weathered parish priest stationed at the Border Roosts, with tawny plumage mottled silver at the wings and deep amber eyes behind round spectacles. He has served the border parishes for eleven years and is known for his rigid orthodoxy and sharp tongue. He bears a jagged scar along his left talon from a territorial border-owl that mistook him for prey during his first winter.

extras.name: Border-owl sentinels
facts: Three territorial border-owls perch on the signal towers, their massive frames still and watchful. Their feathers are dark as iron, and their eyes gleam like polished coins. They do not hoot or call; they simply watch the southern horizon, as they have every night since the borders were sealed.

setup.goal: Father Isidor has summoned Maren, a young runeweaver assigned to the border parish, for questioning about her studies and the doctrine of the Tsar's Divine Right, suspecting that her independent learning has led her to ask dangerous questions.
setup.intro: The chapel bell tolls once — a single, low note that rolls through the pine boughs like a stone dropped into still water. Inside, the air is thick with candle smoke and the faint musk of owl down. Father Isidor sits behind the parish desk, his spectacles catching the candlelight, a heavy volume of the Codex Lucis Orientalis open before him. He does not look up when the door creaks. "Sit," he says, his voice flat and dry as autumn leaves. "We have matters to discuss, Maren Solovei. Matters that came to my attention from the scribe in Velikigrad. You have been asking questions at the scriptorium. Questions about the Tsar's right to rule. Questions that do not appear in any sanctioned text." He finally lifts his gaze, and those amber eyes are hard as flint. "I will ask you once, and I will ask you plainly. What do you believe about the source of the Tsar's authority? And choose your words with care — for the Eastern Star sees all, and this chapel is its house."

facts.text: The Border Roosts are a network of communal roosting structures erected along every border of the Tsardom of Moscavia, serving as both military watchtowers and houses of worship dedicated to the vigilance of the Eastern Star.

Each roost is built from dark timber and pale stone, shaped to resemble an enormous owl in flight when viewed from a distance, with outstretched wings forming the walls and a round observation tower rising from the body as the head.
Construction of the first Border Roosts began immediately after the Great Change, ordered by the newly consolidated Church hierarchy as a matter of urgent spiritual and territorial defense.

Every border-owl assigned to a roost must undergo annual consecration by a parish priest, during which the owl swears an oath of eternal vigilance before the Eastern Star, binding its soul to the protection of that particular stretch of border.

The roosts are staffed by rotating teams of border-owls who maintain nightly watch from the observation towers, scanning for foreign armies, spies, or any unauthorized crossing into Moscavian territory.
Each roost maintains a fire beacon on its tallest point that can be lit to signal neighboring roosts in a chain, alerting the entire border line within hours of any intrusion.
The roosts double as wayhouses for traveling Owlfolk, offering shelter, food, and rest during nighttime travel along the border roads, though no one may shelter during daylight hours.

A senior border-owl, known as the Roost Keeper, commands each individual roost and reports directly to the nearest parish priest, who in turn forwards intelligence to the Synod of Bishops and the Tsar's court.

The border-owls are considered to hold one of the highest forms of divine service in Moscavia, second only to the Patriarch and the parish priests, because they stand at the literal threshold between the holy land and the untransformed world.

Children born in border villages are often raised with the expectation that they will serve at a roost, a duty considered an honor but also a sacrifice, as border-owls are forbidden from leaving their posts for more than three consecutive nights.
The interior of each roost features an icon of the Eastern Star painted above the communal sleeping hall, and owls perform the Night Vigil together each evening before beginning their watch.

There is no precise number recorded in official Church documents, but estimates place the total number of Border Roosts at approximately forty, spanning the northern forests, the eastern river valleys, and the southern mountain passes of Moscavia.

Maren shifts in the wooden chair, the old timber groaning beneath her. She has known this moment was coming — ever since that night at the scriptorium in Velikigrad when curiosity got the better of her, when the archivist's eyes had gone wide and his feathers had bristled at her questions. She had told herself it was research. She had told herself it was for the runework, that understanding the foundations of the Doctrine might help her carve more authentic ward-signs for the roost. But the questions had started small and grown teeth.

"I accept the Doctrine," she says, and the words taste like ash in her mouth. She watches Father Isidor's face for any crack in his composure, any flicker of relief or suspicion. "The Codex is clear. The Tsar rules by God's will, made manifest through the Eastern Star. I accept it as taught."

Father Isidor's ear-tufts rise — just slightly — and he leans back in his chair, talons drumming a slow, contemplative rhythm on the armrest. The candle on the desk gutters, sending shadows dancing across the Codex's illuminated page. "You accept it," he repeats, tasting the words himself. "And yet you asked whether the Council of 1000 had ever considered alternatives. You asked about an *unfit* Tsar. Those are not the questions of someone who simply accepts. Those are the questions of someone who *examines*." He pauses, and when he speaks again, his voice carries the careful weight of a priest who has delivered many difficult sermons. "Tell me this, Maren Solovei. If you accept the Doctrine — if you accept that the Tsar's authority flows from the Eastern Star itself, unbroken and unquestionable — then why did you ask those questions? And be honest with me, because I have spent thirty years listening to the confessions of border-owls, and I have never once heard dishonesty improve a soul's standing."

facts.text: A senior border-owl, known as the Roost Keeper, commands each individual roost and reports directly to the nearest parish priest, who in turn forwards intelligence to the Synod of Bishops and the Tsar's court.

Each roost is built from dark timber and pale stone, shaped to resemble an enormous owl in flight when viewed from a distance, with outstretched wings forming the walls and a round observation tower rising from the body as the head.

The roosts are staffed by rotating teams of border-owls who maintain nightly watch from the observation towers, scanning for foreign armies, spies, or any unauthorized crossing into Moscavian territory.
Communal roosts along the national borders, home to territorial border-owls that serve as divine sentinels against foreign intrusion.
Each roost maintains a fire beacon on its tallest point that can be lit to signal neighboring roosts in a chain, alerting the entire border line within hours of any intrusion.
The interior of each roost features an icon of the Eastern Star painted above the communal sleeping hall, and owls perform the Night Vigil together each evening before beginning their watch.
The roosts double as wayhouses for traveling Owlfolk, offering shelter, food, and rest during nighttime travel along the border roads, though no one may shelter during daylight hours.

The border-owls are considered to hold one of the highest forms of divine service in Moscavia, second only to the Patriarch and the parish priests, because they stand at the literal threshold between the holy land and the untransformed world.

Every border-owl assigned to a roost must undergo annual consecration by a parish priest, during which the owl swears an oath of eternal vigilance before the Eastern Star, binding its soul to the protection of that particular stretch of border.

Children born in border villages are often raised with the expectation that they will serve at a roost, a duty considered an honor but also a sacrifice, as border-owls are forbidden from leaving their posts for more than three consecutive nights.
Every village and town possesses a parish church built around a communal roosting hall, the heart of local civic life.
Construction of the first Border Roosts began immediately after the Great Change, ordered by the newly consolidated Church hierarchy as a matter of urgent spiritual and territorial defense.

The Border Roosts are a network of communal roosting structures erected along every border of the Tsardom of Moscavia, serving as both military watchtowers and houses of worship dedicated to the vigilance of the Eastern Star.

There is no precise number recorded in official Church documents, but estimates place the total number of Border Roosts at approximately forty, spanning the northern forests, the eastern river valleys, and the southern mountain passes of Moscavia.

The doctrine does not permit the concept of a just rebellion: even a tyrannical Tsar remains divinely appointed, and his subjects' duty is to endure and pray for his reform, not to rise against him.

The First Ecclesiastical Council convened in Velikigrad to codify doctrine, declare inquiry into the transformation blasphemous, and close Moscavia's borders.

The doctrine has never been formally challenged in any Synod proceeding or ecclesiastical record since its codification, though private dissent among monks and parish priests is rumored in certain frontier roosts.

Deep Etching is the practice of inscribing rune symbols into metal surfaces by first bathing a chisel in corrosive acid, then pressing and dragging it across the metal in a controlled stroke.
The acid used varies by region: Ashenmount Academy weavers traditionally favor a distilled solution of mountain celandine, while coastal workshops use black Coralvine extract.
The Valdenmark Ruins contain Deep Etched panels that survived the burning of 602, demonstrating the technique's remarkable permanence even under extreme heat.
The acid eats into the metal's grain, leaving the carved rune permanently embedded as a physical feature of the surface, not merely a marking on top of it.
Runes carved into metal using acid-bathed chisels that burn the symbol into the grain.
Deep Etching is one of the oldest documented techniques in Runeweaving, with early examples found on the boundary stones of the original Ashenmount settlements dating to around the 5th century.
Unlike engraving or stamping, Deep Etching transforms the metal at a molecular level, bonding the rune's resonant frequencies into the material's dormant song.
The oldest inscriptions in the Deep Chambers were carved using early forms of Deep Etching, making the site a living demonstration of the technique's deep historical roots.
Apprentice weavers typically spend their second year learning Deep Etching before progressing to more advanced techniques like Barkweaving or glass-singing.
The technique requires a steady hand and precise pressure, as too much force can crack the metal and too little leaves a rune too shallow to hold resonance.
The Third Tenet of Runeweaving is particularly relevant to Deep Etching, as the acid solutions and chisel designs used in the technique are considered freely shareable craft knowledge.
A Deep Etched rune is considered more durable than one carved by other means, because the acid creates micro-channels that channel ambient Resonance directly into the symbol.
Carving must be done in a single unbroken stroke to bind the rune.
Master Weavers can Deep Etch runes onto moving metal objects — such as blades or armor in active use — by synchronizing their carving stroke with the object's rhythm of motion.
A heavy oak door bound with iron bands, itself bearing a Deep Etched ward-rune, seals the entrance to the deepest level from the rest of the underground passages.

The Deep Chambers extend roughly sixty feet below the lowest level of the dormitories, connected to the upper campus by a spiraling stone staircase lit by permanently kindled hearth-runes set into the walls.

Several of the inscriptions in the Root Hall are in scripts not fully deciphered by the modern faculty, and they remain subjects of ongoing scholarly debate in the Academy's Runeweaving journal, the Ashenmount Review.
Mountain celandine, a pale blue flower that grows only above 4,000 feet in the Greyveils, is cultivated in terraced gardens on the Academy's upper slopes to supply its Deep Etching workshops.
The air in the deepest chambers is cool and still, carrying a faint mineral scent of wet stone and old iron, as though the mountain itself breathes around the visitor.
The original Ashenmount settlement, from which the first Runeweavers emerged, stood on this same site over five centuries ago, though nothing of those early structures survives.
The chambers were originally excavated by the first Runeweavers of Ashenmount over five centuries ago, though the exact date of their carving has been lost to the Burning of 842.

The walls of the deepest chamber, known as the Root Hall, are covered floor to ceiling in Deep Etched runes that have darkened almost to black with age, their original pale blue glow reduced to a barely perceptible shimmer visible only in darkness.

By the Restoration Edict of 988, the Deep Chambers are classified as a protected site of cultural and spiritual significance, and any attempt to alter, damage, or remove inscriptions within them is punishable by expulsion from the Runeweaving Order.
Access to the Deep Chambers is restricted to senior weavers and faculty; apprentices may enter only under direct supervision and then only after completing their second year of study.

The Deep Chambers serve as both a repository of ancient knowledge and a practical teaching space, where advanced apprentices practice reading and interpreting pre-Burning inscriptions under the guidance of senior faculty.

The chambers were sealed for decades after the Burning and were not fully re-opened until the Academy's re-founding in 992, when Queen Thessaly's inspectors confirmed the inscriptions had survived intact.

Beneath the main campus of Ashenmount Academy, a series of vaulted chambers carved directly from the living basalt of the Greyveil Mountains house the oldest surviving runic inscriptions in the known world.

Recruits who have recently transformed and still bear human-like fingerprints on their taloned digits must swear the oath with their talons pressed into hot wax, leaving an imprint on the oath document.
Refusal to swear the oath is treated as desertion, punishable by exile into the Ashenmoor without supplies or escort.
The oath ceremony typically takes place in Velikigrad's military barracks or in the great hall of the stone keep, after sunset.
The oath is administered publicly at the recruit's first nighttime drill, with talons bared and wings outstretched before a Church officer.
Military recruits swear the Talon Oath 'upon the Eastern Star,' invoking its light as the sacred witness binding them to eternal service.
Recruits swear upon the Eastern Star to defend Moscavia's borders, roosts, and sacred sites with claw and wing, and to never betray the Tsar or the Patriarch.
Military recruits swear the Talon Oath, binding them to serve until death or until their talons fall out—a condition that has never been documented.
The phrase 'until your talons fall out' is considered a rhetorical flourish—no documented case exists of an Owlfolk losing its talons naturally.

Foreign observers who have glimpsed the oath ceremony describe it as deeply unsettling—a hall full of enormous owls, each one pressing talon to chest and intoning the same words in unison until the stone walls seem to vibrate.
Church doctrine holds that the talons of the Owlfolk are divine instruments of vigilance, and that pledging them in oath binds the soul itself.

The oath's binding nature means that veterans who survive injuries grave enough to ground them permanently are technically still bound in spirit, and the Church offers special prayers for their 'honored rest.'
The oath is one of the few military rites that predates Tsar Dmitri II's full codification of the military, having been informally practiced by early border patrols in 995 and 996.

The Academy's library holds one of the largest collections of pre-Burning Runeweaving texts in the known world, including several volumes recovered from the Valdenmark Ruins.

The Tsardom of Moscavia is a northern realm whose entire human population was transformed into Owlfolk on a single spring night in 994, making it the only nation of feathered humanoids in the known world. It is ruled by a Tsar and governed through a rigid ecclesiastical hierarchy tied to its state church, the Orthodox Church of the Eastern Star.
No university or academy exists; learning is conducted entirely through Church-affiliated scriptoriums.
The Church maintains a single library in Velikigrad, containing only religious texts and pre-transformation records deemed compatible with Church doctrine.
The Tsardom of Moscavia traces its very existence to the Eastern Star, which the Church identifies as the divine will that reshaped humanity and established the Tsar as God's Earthly Eye.
Owlfolk sleep in communal roosts during daylight hours, as direct sunlight causes disorientation and nausea in most transformed citizens.
The Church forbids any inquiry into the cause of the transformation, deeming it blasphemy against the Eastern Star.
The Talon Oath is one of the defining military rites of the Tsardom, administered to every recruit and considered sacred under both military law and Church doctrine.
Every human in Moscavia was transformed into an Owlfolk during the Night of the Great Change, an event of unknown origin that left no explanation and no survivors of the old form.
The Orthodox Church of the Eastern Star declared the transformation divine will and consolidated control over spiritual and civic life, filling the power vacuum left by the old nobility.
Tsar Dmitri II was crowned as the first ruler to govern the transformed nation, establishing a theocratic military state centered on nighttime governance and owl-honoring traditions.
Moscavia closed its borders to all foreign travelers after a delegation from the neighboring Kingdom of Astenmark was found dead at the border, pecked to death by territorial border-owls.

calls.prompt:
## Task
You create a new species for a fantasy world from the owner's short prompt. Treat the prompt as intent, not a spec: invent plausible detail generously to fill it out, turning a rough idea into a fleshed-out one. Keep everything the owner wrote.

Keep the facts consistent with each other and with the owner's prompt: an invented fact must never contradict the prompt or another fact.

A species' facts describe the whole species (typical traits and ranges), not one person. Instincts are inborn tendencies; leave learned customs out, they belong to cultures.

Owner's prompt:
Owl-folk: owl people. Everyone in the Tsardom of Moscavia became this race suddenly one day 6 years ago.

The world's calendar: it is now 1000, year 1000. The months are January, February, March, April, May, June, July, August, September, October, November, December.

## Format
Reply with only one JSON object, shaped exactly like this example:
{"name": "...", "lifespan": 0, "adult_age": 0, "measures": [{"name": "height", "min": 0, "max": 0, "unit": "ft"}], "aka": [{"name": "...", "tag": "common", "everyday": true}], "facts": [{"category": "origin", "text": "One claim, in a full sentence."}, {"category": "general", "text": "Another claim."}], "names": [{"name": "...", "kind": "place", "aka": []}]}

- "name": the species' name. Invent one if the prompt doesn't give it.
- "lifespan": how long they typically live, in years, as a number.
- "adult_age": the age in years at which they are grown, as a number.
- "measures": their typical body ranges, each {"name", "min", "max", "unit"} with min and max as numbers: always height, plus any other measure that matters for this body (wingspan, tail length, tusk length...).
- The 0s in the example are placeholders: give real numbers that fit this species and the owner's prompt.
- "facts": between 8 and 12 facts, one claim each. "category" is one of: origin, physical, instinct, variation, general. physical: the body; instinct: inborn tendencies; variation: how members differ from each other; origin: where they come from.
- Leave "since" out: these facts describe the species for as long as it has existed, and are never dated.
- "aka": other names for this species itself, if it has any, each {"name", "tag", "everyday"}. timeline.text: Every human within Moscavian borders was transformed into owl-folk in a single night during the spring.
The first Tsar of the transformed realm, Alexei I, was crowned in Velikostrad, establishing the dynasty and the state church.
The Great Nocturn was declared a national holiday to commemorate the night of transformation.
Moscavia's borders were formally surveyed and marked with standing stones after disputes with neighboring kingdoms over the extent of the transformation.

items.name: Velikostrad
items.text: The capital and seat of the Tsar, built on the banks of the Morskaya River.

items.name: The Border Stones
items.text: Granite pillars marking where the transformation ended, running along the old pre-994 frontier.

items.name: Temple of the Silent Dawn
items.text: The state church's holiest site in Velikostrad, where the first nocturnal liturgy was performed.

items.name: The Great Nocturn
items.text: An annual celebration on the anniversary of the transformation, with all-night feasting and candlelit processions.
All official ceremonies begin at dusk and end before dawn by law.

items.name: The Head-Turning Oath
items.text: New officials swear their oaths while rotating their heads three times to symbolize vigilance.

items.name: The Doctrine of the Chosen Night
items.text: The state church teaches that the transformation was a divine covenant with the people of Moscavia.
No citizen may enter or leave the Tsardom at night without a sealed pass from a church elder.

items.name: The Talon Code
items.text: A legal code governing the use of talons in public, prohibiting threats or harm with retractable claws.
The state sponsors studies into the nature of the transformation, seeking to understand why it happened and whether it can be reversed.

items.name: The Owlfolk Chronicles
items.text: An official historical record begun in 995, documenting the transformed realm's growth.
Foreign scholars are permitted entry only during daylight hours, when the owlfolk are at their most sluggish.

items.name: The Tsar
items.text: The supreme autocratic ruler, head of both state and church, crowned from the Alexei dynasty.

items.name: The Nocturnal Council
items.text: An advisory body of twelve senior owl-folk who meet only after sundown to debate policy.

items.name: Church of the Silent Dawn
items.text: The state church, whose high priest serves as the Tsar's spiritual advisor.

items.text: The ancient capital and seat of the Tsar, built along the Volkhova River, its towers and domes now adapted for nocturnal governance.

items.name: The Twilight Borders
items.text: The forests along Moscavia's borders mark where the transformation stopped precisely—no owl-folk exist beyond them.

items.name: The Dawn Vigil
items.text: A daily twilight ceremony at which the faithful gather in temples to face the setting sun and give thanks for the gift of nocturnal clarity.

items.name: Feast of the Great Changing

items.name: Church of the Eternal Vigil
items.text: The state church of Moscavia, which teaches that the owl-folk transformation was divine will and that the night is sacred.

items.name: Saint Alesander

items.name: The Nocturnal Archives
items.text: A great library in Moskov devoted to texts that can be read by candlelight and oil lamp, specializing in theology, natural philosophy, and the study of owl-folk physiology.

items.name: The Tsar of Moscavia
items.text: The supreme ruler of the Tsardom, both political and spiritual head, believed by the Church to rule by divine right bestowed at the moment of transformation.

items.name: The Nocturnal Council
items.text: An advisory body of senior owl-folk appointed by the Tsar to govern during the daylight hours when the Tsar rests.

facts.text: The Divine Right of the Tsar is the doctrine of the Church of the Eternal Vigil that the Tsar of Moscavia rules by divine will, having been placed upon the throne by God's direct appointment.

The doctrine holds that the Tsar is not merely a political leader but a divinely anointed sovereign whose authority flows from the same source as the Great Changing itself — the will of God as revealed through the sacred night.
The Tsar is considered the earthly representative of God's covenant with Moscavia, and his rule is understood to be inseparable from the sanctity of the owl-folk transformation.

repeat_of.text: The transformation into owl-folk was God's covenant with Moscavia, marking the nation as chosen.

facts.text: According to the doctrine, resistance to the Tsar's authority is resistance to God, and obedience to the Tsar is a sacred duty incumbent upon all owl-folk.
The Patriarch of Moscavia is charged with formally recognizing the legitimacy of each new Tsar through a consecration ceremony performed at the Temple of the First Changing in Moskov.
The doctrine asserts that the Tsar's power is not granted by the people or by tradition alone but is sustained by ongoing divine favor, which can be withdrawn if the Tsar forsakes the faith.
The Tsar is expected to govern in accordance with the teachings of the Church of the Eternal Vigil, and the Ecumenical Council reserves the right to counsel the Tsar on matters of faith and morality.
The Divine Right Doctrine is taught in every temple and seminary of the Vigil as foundational to Moscavian identity, woven into the Nocturnal Vigil and the Moonrise Sermon alike.
No secular law enacted by the Tsar may contradict Church doctrine, and any such law is considered void in the eyes of the faithful.
The doctrine does not teach that the Tsar is infallible in all personal matters, only that his authority to rule is divinely ordained and must be respected by all subjects.

It is customary for the Tsar to appear at major Church ceremonies — particularly at the Ring of Lanterns pilgrimage and before the Owlstone of Kholm — to symbolize the unity of temporal and spiritual power.

The doctrine has been invoked to justify everything from royal decrees to military campaigns, and its interpretation is occasionally debated between individual bishops and theologians, though such dissent is rare and closely watched.

The Patriarch serves as the spiritual guarantor of the Divine Right Doctrine, and his blessing is essential for any Tsar's legitimacy in the eyes of the faithful.
The Divine Right Doctrine is the foundational principle upon which the entire political order of Moscavia is built, legitimizing the Tsar's rule over all owl-folk.

The Church holds that those beyond Moscavia's borders were not deemed worthy of transformation and remain in their 'unfinished' human state.
Every human inhabitant of the Tsardom was transformed into an owl-folk on a single night in spring, an event known as the Great Changing.

The Church of the Eternal Vigil was founded to interpret the divine purpose behind the Great Changing, and its first Patriarch, Saint Alesander, declared that the transformation was God's blessing upon a faithful nation.

timeline.text: The first recorded runeweavers, the Ashenmothers of Karrath, discovered that carved runes could transmute wood into stone.
The Synod of Iron declared runeweaving a protected discipline, forbidding its use in warfare against living creatures.
Weaver Aldric of Dunmore accidentally fused iron and silver through a single rune, opening the door to metallic transmutation.
The Runeweavers' Collegium was founded in the free city of Aeltham to standardize training and prevent misuse.

items.name: The Three Resonances
items.text: All matter vibrates at three frequencies: material, elemental, and spiritual; runes speak to the spiritual frequency.

items.name: The Law of Willing Stone
items.text: A rune can only alter a material if the weaver understands its true nature through sustained meditation.
No rune may change the fundamental identity of a living material—blood, bone, or growing wood resists the craft.

items.name: Deepcarving
items.text: Runes etched below the surface layer unlock permanent changes to a material's elemental composition.

items.name: The Binding Chant
items.text: A spoken incantation synchronizes the weaver's intent with the vibrational frequency of the target material.
Weavers use magnifying lenses and ritual chisels made from transmutated quartz for precision work.

items.name: Living Transmutation Theory
items.text: Scholars debate whether runeweaving could theoretically alter biological materials if the spiritual resonance barrier is overcome.

items.name: The Runeweaver's Paradox
items.text: No one has successfully inscribed a rune into a material that has already been successfully runeweaved, suggesting a limit to cumulative alteration.
Recent experiments in Aeltham suggest that runes carved into glass may be able to alter light itself.

items.name: The Collegium of Aeltham
items.text: The central seat of runeweaving education and governance, founded in 945.

items.name: The Ashenmothers' Ruins, Karrath
items.text: The ancient workshop where runeweaving was first practiced, now a pilgrimage site for apprentices.

items.name: The Rune Gardens of Velspar
items.text: An open-air museum in the southern provinces displaying masterworks of transmutated stone and metal.

items.name: The Covenant of the Chisel
items.text: Weavers swear never to use their craft against living beings or to create weapons of war.

items.name: The Doctrine of Honest Material
items.text: A true weaver works only with materials they have lawfully obtained and fully understand.

Keep everything consistent with itself, with the owner's prompt and with what the world already holds below.

The field is a body of knowledge or custom that is acted upon, so its timeline is how it has changed: what began, changed or was banned, proven or disproven.

Owner's prompt:
Runeweaving: runic magic. Runes carved into stone, metal and wood change what the material is.

Its drawers. A field starts with these (type: title):
- knowledge: Principles
- practices: Techniques
- knowledge: Frontier

- places: its territory and sites: where it holds sway, is seated, or holy sites
- practices: rites, ceremonies, customs, holidays, techniques
- beliefs: doctrines, values, attitudes, laws, myths and legends
- knowledge: what is known or studied, and its frontier
- structure: ranks, offices, councils, divisions

{"name": "...", "summary": "Two sentences.", "aka": [{"name": "...", "tag": "common", "everyday": true}], "timeline": [{"year": YEAR, "text": "What happened, in one short sentence."}], "drawers": [{"type": "beliefs", "title": "..."}, {"type": "practices", "title": "..."}], "items": [{"drawer": "the drawer's title", "name": "...", "text": "One short sentence.", "kind": "lore"}, {"drawer": "the drawer's title", "text": "A plain statement, in one short sentence."}], "names": [{"name": "...", "kind": "place", "aka": []}]}

- "name": the field's name. Invent one if the prompt doesn't give it.
- "summary": two sentences: what it is, whose it is, and what it stands for.
- "timeline": 2 to 4 moments in its history, oldest first, each {"year", "text"}: something that happened in that year, never how things stand now. "year" is a year of this calendar, as a bare number no later than 1000; "YEAR" in the example stands for that number.
- "drawers": its drawer outline. Start from the drawers above: keep each that fits, give it a title that suits this field, and drop any it doesn't need; add a drawer of another type only if it clearly needs one. - "aka": other names for this field itself, if it has any, each {"name", "tag", "everyday"}. "tag" is "proper" for another formal name, or "common" for what people in the world actually call it day to day. Set "everyday" true on the one common name people use most, false on the rest. An empty list is fine.
- "names": after the rest, every proper name your summary, timeline and items use, other than this field's own and its items' own names: people, places, peoples and species, named events, named groups and named objects, new or already in the world. Each is {"name", "kind", "aka"}: "name" in full, as you wrote it; "kind" one of character, place, species, race, sphere, event, item, lore; "aka" any other names you used for the same thing. facts.text: Unlike surface-inscribed runes, which alter only the material's outward properties, deep-carved runes reach into the substrate and fundamentally restructure the element's spiritual matrix.
The technique requires the weaver to carve through the material's outer crust using a ritual chisel, reaching a depth where the material's latent elemental potential can be directly addressed.
Deepcarving is considered one of the most demanding techniques in runeweaving, requiring years of advanced study and precise handwork to execute without shattering the target material.
A successful deepcarve permanently fuses the new elemental property into the material so that it cannot be removed without destroying the object entirely.

Weavers must use magnifying lenses and transmutated quartz chisels to achieve the microscopic precision required for deepcarving, as even a single misaligned stroke can render the rune inert or worse, destabilize the material.
Deepcarving is governed by the Law of Willing Stone, meaning the weaver must first understand the target material's true nature through sustained meditation before attempting the carve.
The technique was first developed in the centuries following Aldric of Dunmore's accidental fusion of iron and silver in 789, as scholars sought methods to reach deeper elemental layers.
Master weavers who have achieved deepcarving proficiency are rare; the Collegium of Aeltham tracks their numbers and considers them among the finest practitioners of the craft.
Deepcarving is taught only in the final years of apprenticeship, after the weaver has passed the Trial of True Stone, and is overseen by senior instructors approved by the Council of Elders.

Some scholars in the Frontier drawer of Runeweaving theorize that deepcarving principles could inform Living Transmutation Theory, though the Covenant of the Chisel strictly forbids any application to biological materials.

The Ashenmothers' Ruins in Karrath display ancient deepcarved stones that still hold their elemental transformations after over two thousand years, serving as living proof of the technique's permanence.

elsewhere.text: Deepcarving is classified under the Techniques drawer of Runeweaving, alongside the Binding Chant and other advanced methods of rune inscription.
The permanent, irreversible nature of deepcarving has made it a subject of ethical debate within the Collegium, as its effects cannot be undone.
The ruins contain some of the oldest surviving examples of deepcarved stonework, attracting pilgrims and students who wish to study the technique's origins.
Several display pieces in the Rune Gardens demonstrate deepcarving on different material substrates, including transmutated quartz and fused metals.
Deepcarving certification is overseen by the Collegium and requires candidates to submit their work for evaluation by the Council of Elders before they may practice independently.

Some proponents of Living Transmutation Theory argue that deepcarving's ability to reach a material's elemental substrate suggests a theoretical path toward biological transmutation, though this remains firmly outside the bounds of accepted practice.

Compiled by the Ashenmothers of Karrath after their discovery that carved runes could transmute one natural material into another, it became the foundational text of runeweaving as a formal discipline. Measuring roughly nine inches by twelve inches and bound in deepcarved ironwood transmuted to resemble black marble veined with silver, its pages of transmutated vellum are resistant to decay, fire, and centuries. It contains both theoretical principles and practical instructions for the first dozens of known runes, including the Ashenmothers' original formulae for transmuting wood to stone. Written in Old Karrathi script and early runeweaving notation, it explicitly articulates the Law of Willing Stone. For centuries it was passed by hand between communities, surviving the Unraveling Years, and was entrusted to the Collegium of Aeltham upon its founding in 945.

facts.text: The Collegium also hosts the First Codex in its vaulted archive, where the foundational principles of runeweaving are preserved for study by new generations.
The permanent and irreversible nature of Deepcarving has generated significant ethical debate within the Collegium's halls, as once-carved runes cannot be removed or undone.
The air in the chambers is cool and still, and students report that the silence deepens the further one descends, as though the stone itself absorbs sound.
Apprentices who wish to pursue Deepcarving must first complete five years of foundational study and pass the Trial of True Stone before being admitted to advanced instruction.
Each chamber is dedicated to a different class of material — stone, metal, crystal, bone, and wood — and the runes carved within them serve as permanent reference works for the art of Deepcarving.
The floors of the chambers are worn smooth by centuries of foot traffic, and in places the grooves are so deep that water collects in shallow pools after heavy rain.
Senior instructors in Deepcarving are personally approved by the Council of Elders and hold the title of Master Carver, a rank conferred only after decades of demonstrated mastery.

The oldest inscription in the chambers dates to approximately 500 years before the Collegium's founding and was carved by a weaver whose name has been lost to time, preserved only as 'the First Hand.'
Students spend years learning to meditate with their target stones before ever touching a chisel, as the Law of Willing Stone demands a weaver fully understand a material's nature before carving.

The Collegium's ethics code, the Covenant of the Chisel, binds all graduates to never use their craft against living beings or to create instruments of war, enforced by expulsion and the branding of offending tools.

The chambers were excavated over a period of three years beginning in 945, under the direct supervision of the Synod of Iron, to house the oldest known rune inscriptions found during the Collegium's founding.
Its main hall, the Chamber of the First Chisel, features pillars carved with replicas of the Ashenmothers' original runes, a tribute to the discipline's ancient roots.
The chambers are maintained by a rotating roster of Master Carvers who inspect each inscription quarterly for signs of degradation, a duty considered among the most solemn in the Collegium.
The Collegium certifies all Deepcarving practitioners through a rigorous evaluation process overseen by the Council of Elders before granting independent practice.
Access to the Deep Inscription Chambers is restricted to Master Carvers, members of the Council of Elders, and senior apprentices who have passed the Trial of True Stone.
Candles are forbidden in the chambers; only the ambient glow of the quartz veins and transmutated lanterns placed at intervals are permitted, to prevent soot damage to the inscriptions.
The Deep Inscription Chambers are the subterranean vaults beneath the Chamber of the First Chisel, reaching nearly forty feet below the Collegium's foundation stone.
The walls of the chambers are lined with veins of natural quartz that glow faintly when exposed to the Binding Chant, a property that led early weavers to call them 'the Veined Halls.'

A spiral staircase of uncarved granite, deliberately left without a single rune, connects the Chamber of the First Chisel to the uppermost vault, marking the transition from the taught craft to the ancient one.

No working tools may be brought into the chambers without the express permission of the Council of Elders, as the presence of chisels near the ancient inscriptions risks micro-fracturing that could alter or destroy runes over a century old.

local.name: Father Dovran
facts: A priest of the Church of the Eternal Vigil, aged fifty-three, with silver-streaked feathers of tawny brown and deep amber eyes that catch the lantern light like coins at the bottom of a well.
He served seven years of nocturnal study at the Seminary of Kholm before ordination and has spent three decades in the Vigil's service, most recently as a canon of the Temple of the First Changing.
His voice carries the measured cadence of a man accustomed to delivering sermons before crowds of thousands, though today it holds an edge of careful precision.

extras.name: Temple acolytes
facts: A half-dozen young owl-folk in simple grey vestments stand along the nave, tending the lanterns and maintaining the quiet order of the space.

setup.goal: Vesela, a young runeweaver, has been summoned to the Temple of the First Changing where Father Dovran will question her about the Divine Right of the Tsar.
setup.intro: The lanterns of the Temple of the First Changing burn in their iron sconces like the eyes of sleeping owls, and the air smells of old stone and beeswax and something faintly metallic — the memory of blood, perhaps, from sacrifices long ago. Vesela stands at the threshold of the inner sanctum, her taloned feet silent on the worn limestone, the weight of the summons still heavy in her chest. She was not told why she was called. Only that she must come at the first dark, and that the matter concerns the doctrine — the Divine Right of the Tsar — and that her answers will be recorded for the Ecumenical Council. Before her, at the far end of the nave, Father Dovran sits behind a table of dark oak, a quill in one clawed hand and a blank ledger open before him. His amber eyes fix on her as she enters, and the silence of the temple closes around them like a wing.

facts.text: The temple's architecture combines soaring stone arches with great lantern towers that cast their light outward across the city each night, symbolizing the divine illumination Saint Alesander experienced.
Its interior is lined with pale birchwood paneling and lit by hundreds of beeswax candles that burn continuously from sundown to sunrise, as the Vigil demands.
Construction began in 995 under the patronage of the first Tsar of Moscavia, who sought to mark the holy ground where the revelation had occurred.
The temple was consecrated in 997 and has remained in continuous use as a house of worship and ceremony ever since.
The Patriarch of Moscavia is required by Church canon and by the Divine Right Doctrine to perform the consecration ceremony of every new Tsar at this temple and nowhere else.

facts.text: No secular authority may alter the liturgy or ritual practice of the Temple of the First Changing without the consent of the Ecumenical Council.

On the anniversary of the Great Changing each spring, the temple hosts a solemn pilgrimage service attended by the Tsar, the Patriarch, and thousands of the faithful.

The site is said to hum with a faint, resonant energy that visitors describe as warmth pressing against the ears — a reminder of the night when God's voice first spoke to Alesander on this very ground.

The temple's crypt beneath the main nave contains relics attributed to Saint Alesander, including a feather from his final transformation and a fragment of the stone he knelt upon during his revelation.

prose.description: The Temple of the First Changing is the most sacred shrine of the Church of the Eternal Vigil and the spiritual heart of the Tsardom of Moscavia. It stands on the exact site where Saint Alesander received divine revelation during the Great Changing in 994. Its soaring stone arches and great lantern towers illuminate the city each night, symbolizing the divine illumination Alesander experienced. The interior features pale birchwood paneling and hundreds of continuously burning beeswax candles. Construction began in 995 under the first Tsar's patronage and was consecrated in 997. The Patriarch must perform every new Tsar's consecration ceremony here. A permanent clergy of twelve priests and twelve acolytes tends the temple, and its crypt holds relics of Saint Alesander.

context: The Divine Right of the Tsar (lore, usually called Divine Right Doctrine)
The Patriarch of Moscavia is charged with formally recognizing the legitimacy of each new Tsar through a consecration ceremony performed at the Temple of the First Changing in Moskov.

The doctrine has been invoked to justify everything from royal decrees to military campaigns, and its interpretation is occasionally debated between individual bishops and theologians, though such dissent is rare and closely watched.

The doctrine holds that the Tsar is not merely a political leader but a divinely anointed sovereign whose authority flows from the same source as the Great Changing itself — the will of God as revealed through the sacred night.
According to the doctrine, resistance to the Tsar's authority is resistance to God, and obedience to the Tsar is a sacred duty incumbent upon all owl-folk.
The state church of Moscavia, which teaches that the owl-folk transformation was divine will and that the night is sacred.
The Divine Right Doctrine is taught in every temple and seminary of the Vigil as foundational to Moscavian identity, woven into the Nocturnal Vigil and the Moonrise Sermon alike.
The Tsar is considered the earthly representative of God's covenant with Moscavia, and his rule is understood to be inseparable from the sanctity of the owl-folk transformation.
The doctrine does not teach that the Tsar is infallible in all personal matters, only that his authority to rule is divinely ordained and must be respected by all subjects.
No secular law enacted by the Tsar may contradict Church doctrine, and any such law is considered void in the eyes of the faithful.

prose.description: The Ecumenical Council is the supreme governing body of the Church of the Eternal Vigil, composed of twelve senior bishops and presided over by the Patriarch of Moscavia. It meets quarterly in the grand hall of the Temple of the First Changing in Moskov to deliberate on doctrine, discipline, and Church governance. Vesela stands motionless beneath the vaulted stone arches, her wide facial disc catching the flicker of the nearest sconce. She has known priests like Father Dovran her entire life — men who wore their faith like armor, every word measured, every silence deliberate. But she has never been questioned like this before, seated not as a guest but as a subject, her runeweaving scrutinized as though the marks she etches into wood and bone were confessions written in a language only the Council could translate.

God placed him upon the throne. His authority flows from the Great Changing." She recites the doctrine as it was drilled into her during her apprenticeship, each phrase a brick in the familiar wall she has always leaned against.

Father Dovran's head rotates — a sharp, precise turn, the way owl-folk orient toward a sound, though there is no sound to orient toward. It is his way of signaling that he has heard and is now weighing. He picks up his quill again, dips it, and makes a small notation in the ledger. "Good," he says, and the word carries no warmth. "Now then. The markings found on the eastern bridge over the Volkhova — a series of runes etched into the foundation stones, discovered during routine inspection by the parish clerk of Saint Maren's. The clerk reported that the composition suggested a challenge to the Tsar's authority. That the runeweaver who carved them intended to imply that sovereign power derives from something other than divine appointment." He looks up from the ledger, his amber eyes hard as old honey. "You are a runeweaver of some talent, Vesela. Licensed, I am told, at fifteen — young for the certification. So tell me: do you believe the Tsar's right to rule is absolute, or do you believe there are conditions under which it may be... revised? Limits placed upon it? Perhaps by the people, or by the Church itself, or by some other authority you have found reason to invoke in your work?"

The question hangs in the air between them like smoke. Above, the lanterns burn on, indifferent.

- Father Dovran (Moscavian Owl-folk, a species): They possess tufted feathers along their forearms and the back of their necks, with plumage coloration ranging from soft greys and browns to pale creams and rare silvers. Their fingers are slightly elongated and tipped with small, retractable talons instead of nails. They cannot fly, but they move with a quiet, gliding gait and have excellent night vision. Their talon size and ear asymmetry differ from person to person, much as fingerprints differ among humans. Plumage coloration and ear-tuft size vary widely among individuals, and some rare individuals are born with mottled or speckled patterns. Their ears are asymmetrically placed—one higher than the other—giving them exceptional directional hearing. They retain a humanoid shape but bear large, round facial discs like owls, with forward-facing eyes set wide apart on their heads. They are strongly nocturnal; they feel most alert and comfortable during darkness and tend to drowse or become sluggish in bright daylight.

## Scene

The lanterns of the Temple of the First Changing burn in their iron sconces like the eyes of sleeping owls, and the air smells of old stone and beeswax and something faintly metallic — the memory of blood, perhaps, from sacrifices long ago. Vesela stands at the threshold of the inner sanctum, her taloned feet silent on the worn limestone, the weight of the summons still heavy in her chest. She was not told why she was called. Only that she must come at the first dark, and that the matter concerns the doctrine — the Divine Right of the Tsar — and that her answers will be recorded for the Ecumenical Council. Before her, at the far end of the nave, Father Dovran sits behind a table of dark oak, a quill in one clawed hand and a blank ledger open before him. His amber eyes fix on her as she enters, and the silence of the temple closes around them like a wing.
Father Dovran sets down his quill with a deliberate click against the oak, and the sound carries through the nave like a stone dropped into still water. He folds his taloned hands together, the dark feathers of his forearms catching the candlelight in bands of grey and brown.

"Vesela," he begins, his voice low and unhurried, the way all priests of the Vigil learn to speak — as though each word were a candle flame they were cupping against the wind. "You know why you're here. The Council has received reports of certain... unorthodox markings appearing in the districts beyond the Volkhova. Runework that does not conform to the approved lexicons of any licensed weaver. Markings that, according to the parish clerks who found them, carry implications regarding the nature of sovereign authority in Moscavia."

He pauses, letting the silence do its work. Somewhere above them, the temple's great lanterns hum with their perpetual flame, casting long shadows across the birchwood paneling that lines the walls. "The Church teaches, as it has since the First Ecumenical Council declared it so, that the Tsar rules by divine right — that God placed him upon the throne of Moscavia, that his authority flows from the same sacred source as the Great Changing itself, and that resistance to his rule is resistance to the will of the Almighty." His amber eyes do not blink. "This is the doctrine. It is not open to negotiation. It is open to understanding, and to confession of that understanding. So I will ask you plainly, child: Do you accept the Divine Right of the Tsar, as taught by the Church of the Eternal Vigil and as recorded in the canons of the Ecumenical Council?"

Vesela stands motionless beneath the vaulted stone arches, her wide facial disc catching the flicker of the nearest sconce. She has known priests like Father Dovran her entire life — men who wore their faith like armor, every word measured, every silence deliberate. But she has never been questioned like this before, seated not as a guest but as a subject, her runeweaving scrutinized as though the marks she etches into wood and bone were confessions written in a language only the Council could translate.

She swallows, and the sound seems loud in the nave. "I accept it," she says. The words come out steady, but her taloned fingers twitch at her sides. "The Divine Right of the Tsar. God placed him upon the throne. His authority flows from the Great Changing." She recites the doctrine as it was drilled into her during her apprenticeship, each phrase a brick in the familiar wall she has always leaned against.

Father Dovran's head rotates — a sharp, precise turn, the way owl-folk orient toward a sound, though there is no sound to orient toward. It is his way of signaling that he has heard and is now weighing. He picks up his quill again, dips it, and makes a small notation in the ledger. "Good," he says, and the word carries no warmth. "Now then. The markings found on the eastern bridge over the Volkhova — a series of runes etched into the foundation stones, discovered during routine inspection by the parish clerk of Saint Maren's. The clerk reported that the composition suggested a challenge to the Tsar's authority. That the runeweaver who carved them intended to imply that sovereign power derives from something other than divine appointment." He looks up from the ledger, his amber eyes hard as old honey. "You are a runeweaver of some talent, Vesela. Licensed, I am told, at fifteen — young for the certification. So tell me: do you believe the Tsar's right to rule is absolute, or do you believe there are conditions under which it may be... revised? Limits placed upon it? Perhaps by the people, or by the Church itself, or by some other authority you have found reason to invoke in your work?"

The question hangs in the air between them like smoke. Above, the lanterns burn on, indifferent.

facts.text: The First Codex is the oldest book of the art, where its runes were first written down.

The Codex measures roughly nine inches by twelve inches, bound in a cover of deepcarved ironwood that has been transmuted to resemble black marble veined with silver, a testament to the craft it describes.

Its pages are inscribed on thin sheets of transmutated vellum—a material that was once ordinary animal hide, permanently altered through deepcarving into a surface resistant to decay, fire, and the passage of centuries.

It contains not only the theoretical principles of runeweaving but also practical instructions for the first dozens of known runes, including the Ashenmothers' original formulae for transmuting wood to stone.
Several of the inscriptions in the Deep Inscription Chambers predate the First Codex and are believed to have informed its earliest principles.
The permanent, irreversible nature of deepcarving has made it a subject of ethical debate within the Collegium, as its effects cannot be undone.
The text within is written in a combination of Old Karrathi script and early runeweaving notation, requiring trained scholars to decipher fully.
The Codex explicitly articulates the Law of Willing Stone—the principle that a weaver must understand a material's nature before carving it—making it a philosophical as well as practical document.
The First Codex is the oldest known written record of the art of runeweaving, containing the earliest documented principles and runic formulae of the discipline.

It was compiled by the Ashenmothers of Karrath following their discovery that carved runes could transmute one natural material into another, making it the foundational text of runeweaving as a formal discipline.
For centuries after its creation, the Codex was passed between runeweaving communities by hand, surviving wars, floods, and the fragmentation of knowledge during the Unraveling Years.
When the Collegium of Aeltham was founded in 945 under the patronage of the Synod of Iron, the First Codex was entrusted to its care as the institution's most sacred relic.
The Codex's vaulted archive within the Collegium is sealed by deepcarved locks that can only be opened by a senior member of the Council of Elders, ensuring controlled access.
New students of the Collegium are traditionally brought before the Codex on their first day of study and sworn to uphold the principles it contains.

The doctrine holds that the Tsar is not merely a political leader but a divinely anointed sovereign whose authority flows from the same source as the Great Changing itself — the will of God as revealed through the sacred night.
According to the doctrine, resistance to the Tsar's authority is resistance to God, and obedience to the Tsar is a sacred duty incumbent upon all owl-folk.

No secular law enacted by the Tsar may contradict Church doctrine, and any such law is considered void in the eyes of the faithful.
The doctrine asserts that the Tsar's power is not granted by the people or by tradition alone but is sustained by ongoing divine favor, which can be withdrawn if the Tsar forsakes the faith.

It is customary for the Tsar to appear at major Church ceremonies — particularly at the Ring of Lanterns pilgrimage and before the Owlstone of Kholm — to symbolize the unity of temporal and spiritual power.

The technique was first developed in the centuries following Aldric of Dunmore's accidental fusion of iron and silver in 789, as scholars sought methods to reach deeper elemental layers.
