The White Talon's barracks are housed within the innermost ring of Moskov itself, adjacent to the Tsar's palace, in buildings oriented so that every chamber faces north to avoid the morning sun.
The White Talon serves as the Tsar's personal guard during ceremonial processions and state occasions, marching in formation at the vanguard of the royal retinue.
The Tsardom keeps a standing army of owl-folk, organized into regiments such as the White Talon and the Frosted Wing.

The Frosted Wing, a sister regiment of the standing army, draws its recruits from the commoner owl-folk and serves primarily as a cavalry force, while the White Talon remains an infantry unit devoted to close protection and urban defense.
The regiment is led by a Colonel-General appointed by the Tsar, who must be a direct descendant of the House of Volkov, the dynasty from which the current Tsar claims descent.

Recruits must trace their lineage to one of the twelve Great Houses that existed in the Tsardom prior to the Great Changing of 994, and must bear predominantly white plumage as proof of noble descent.
Soldiers of the White Talon wear armor crafted from pale leather and silver wire, light enough for rapid movement but stiffened with bone plates at the shoulders and shins.

Every soldier of the White Talon is expected to have received formal training in the liberal arts before entering military service, including reading, calligraphy, and the study of Moscavian scripture.
The White Talon is an elite infantry regiment of the Moscavian standing army, composed entirely of owl-folk transformed from the old human nobility of the Tsardom.
The regiment's standard depicts a white owl's talon clutching a silver lantern against a field of deep indigo, symbolizing the Tsar's light held fast through the darkest night.

Regimental discipline is enforced through a code derived from the Church's teachings on vigilance and duty, and transgressions are judged not only by the Colonel-General but by a chaplain of the Church of the Eternal Vigil attached to the regiment.

In the six years since its founding, the White Talon has seen combat only once — during the suppression of the Velikiye Revolt in the outer ring of Novosel, where its discipline and training allowed it to restore order without collapsing into the indiscriminate violence that marked the Frosted Wing's deployment in the same theater.

The permanent and irreversible nature of Deepcarving has generated significant ethical debate within the Collegium's halls, as once-carved runes cannot be removed or undone.
The air in the chambers is cool and still, and students report that the silence deepens the further one descends, as though the stone itself absorbs sound.
Apprentices who wish to pursue Deepcarving must first complete five years of foundational study and pass the Trial of True Stone before being admitted to advanced instruction.
Each chamber is dedicated to a different class of material — stone, metal, crystal, bone, and wood — and the runes carved within them serve as permanent reference works for the art of Deepcarving.
The floors of the chambers are worn smooth by centuries of foot traffic, and in places the grooves are so deep that water collects in shallow pools after heavy rain.
Senior instructors in Deepcarving are personally approved by the Council of Elders and hold the title of Master Carver, a rank conferred only after decades of demonstrated mastery.

The oldest inscription in the chambers dates to approximately 500 years before the Collegium's founding and was carved by a weaver whose name has been lost to time, preserved only as 'the First Hand.'
Students spend years learning to meditate with their target stones before ever touching a chisel, as the Law of Willing Stone demands a weaver fully understand a material's nature before carving.

The Collegium's ethics code, the Covenant of the Chisel, binds all graduates to never use their craft against living beings or to create instruments of war, enforced by expulsion and the branding of offending tools.

The chambers were excavated over a period of three years beginning in 945, under the direct supervision of the Synod of Iron, to house the oldest known rune inscriptions found during the Collegium's founding.
Its main hall, the Chamber of the First Chisel, features pillars carved with replicas of the Ashenmothers' original runes, a tribute to the discipline's ancient roots.
The chambers are maintained by a rotating roster of Master Carvers who inspect each inscription quarterly for signs of degradation, a duty considered among the most solemn in the Collegium.
The Collegium certifies all Deepcarving practitioners through a rigorous evaluation process overseen by the Council of Elders before granting independent practice.
Access to the Deep Inscription Chambers is restricted to Master Carvers, members of the Council of Elders, and senior apprentices who have passed the Trial of True Stone.
Candles are forbidden in the chambers; only the ambient glow of the quartz veins and transmutated lanterns placed at intervals are permitted, to prevent soot damage to the inscriptions.
The Deep Inscription Chambers are the subterranean vaults beneath the Chamber of the First Chisel, reaching nearly forty feet below the Collegium's foundation stone.
The walls of the chambers are lined with veins of natural quartz that glow faintly when exposed to the Binding Chant, a property that led early weavers to call them 'the Veined Halls.'

A spiral staircase of uncarved granite, deliberately left without a single rune, connects the Chamber of the First Chisel to the uppermost vault, marking the transition from the taught craft to the ancient one.

No working tools may be brought into the chambers without the express permission of the Council of Elders, as the presence of chisels near the ancient inscriptions risks micro-fracturing that could alter or destroy runes over a century old.

For centuries after its creation, the Codex was passed between runeweaving communities by hand, surviving wars, floods, and the fragmentation of knowledge during the Unraveling Years.
The Synod of Iron declared runeweaving a protected discipline, forbidding its use in warfare against living creatures.

The technique was first developed in the centuries following Aldric of Dunmore's accidental fusion of iron and silver in 789, as scholars sought methods to reach deeper elemental layers.
The Runeweavers' Collegium was founded in the free city of Aeltham to standardize training and prevent misuse.

When the Collegium of Aeltham was founded in 945 under the patronage of the Synod of Iron, the First Codex was entrusted to its care as the institution's most sacred relic.
New students of the Collegium are traditionally brought before the Codex on their first day of study and sworn to uphold the principles it contains.
The Codex's vaulted archive within the Collegium is sealed by deepcarved locks that can only be opened by a senior member of the Council of Elders, ensuring controlled access.
The walls of the chambers are lined with veins of natural quartz that glow faintly when exposed to the Binding Chant, a property that led early weavers to call them 'the Veined Halls.'
Access to the Deep Inscription Chambers is restricted to Master Carvers, members of the Council of Elders, and senior apprentices who have passed the Trial of True Stone.

No working tools may be brought into the chambers without the express permission of the Council of Elders, as the presence of chisels near the ancient inscriptions risks micro-fracturing that could alter or destroy runes over a century old.
The Collegium certifies all Deepcarving practitioners through a rigorous evaluation process overseen by the Council of Elders before granting independent practice.

Every human inhabitant of the Tsardom of Moscavia was transformed into an owl-folk on a single night in the spring of the year 994.

They have a deep instinct to orient themselves toward sound, turning their heads in sharp, precise rotations to locate noise sources.

Their talon size and ear asymmetry differ from person to person, much as fingerprints differ among humans.
Six years after the transformation, in the year 1000, the Owl-folk have fully adapted to their new natures and have rebuilt their society accordingly.
They are strongly nocturnal; they feel most alert and comfortable during darkness and tend to drowse or become sluggish in bright daylight.

Their ears are asymmetrically placed—one higher than the other—giving them exceptional directional hearing.

The Ashenmere rune dialect, rediscovered in 947, suggests a third resonance law that contradicts Aelberth's teachings.
A rune's power depends on the material's natural affinity with the glyph's meaning.

Forcing a rune onto a material that resists it — what weavers call 'compulsion' — is considered a sin against craft, as it corrupts the inscription and risks damaging the weaver's own connection to the art.
The material has a right to refuse the rune; forcing an inscription is considered a sin against craft.

clusters.owner: The Divine Right of the Tsar

Trade with neighboring Valdmark, Keshra, and the Southern Reach continues, though diplomatic relations have been complicated by the fact that eared owl-folk—descended from diluted Moscavian bloodlines—now form the majority of Owl-folk populations in those lands.

clusters.owner: The Divine Right of the Tsar
clusters.text: The Tsardom of Moscavia is a vast northern kingdom stretching across rolling forests, frozen rivers, and open steppe, bordered to the west by Valdmark, to the south by Keshra, and to the southeast by the Free Cities of the Southern Reach.

The Tsardom of Moscavia is a vast northern kingdom stretching across rolling forests, frozen rivers, and rolling steppe, bordered to the west by Valdmark, to the south by Keshra, and to the southeast by the Free Cities of the Southern Reach.

Founded in the early centuries before the current reckoning, the Tsardom has been ruled by a succession of Tsars and Tsarinas who claim divine right through the blessing of the Church of the Eternal Light.
The Tsardom was founded in the early centuries before the current reckoning, with the Church of the Eternal Light established by the first Tsar.
It also establishes the ethical framework governing Runeweaving, including the principle that a material has the right to refuse an inscription and that no rune may be carved for profit alone.
Deepcarving is governed by the same ethical principles as all Runeweaving: a material has the right to refuse the inscription, and no rune may be carved for profit alone.
All objects possess a latent rune signature that can be amplified or redirected.
Theoretical models suggest the Unwritten Rune would function by accessing and overwriting an object's latent rune signature entirely, rather than simply amplifying or redirecting it.
The First Codex of Aelberth is compiled, standardizing 24 foundational runes.

The First Codex of Aelberth, which standardized the 24 foundational runes, makes no mention of the Unwritten Rune, leading scholars to debate whether it was unknown in Aelberth's time or deliberately omitted.
Theoretical rune that could rewrite an object's fundamental nature entirely; no confirmed instance exists.

The Unwritten Rune is a theoretical rune that, if successfully inscribed, could rewrite an object's fundamental nature entirely — not merely enhance it, but replace its essential identity with something new.
Runes etched below the surface of a material using enchanted chisels for lasting, powerful effects.

Deepcarving is the practice of etching runes below the surface of a material using enchanted chisels, producing inscriptions that are more durable and carry greater magical potency than surface-level markings.

The Church of the Eternal Light is the state religion of the Tsardom of Moscavia, claiming divine right for the Tsar and Tsarina through the blessing of the Eternal Light; its doctrines center on the belief that the Light is the source of all creation and that the Owl-folk transformation of 994 was a holy act of illumination.

The Church of the Eternal Light remains the state religion of the Tsardom of Moscavia, claiming divine right for the Tsar through the blessing of the Eternal Light, with doctrines centering on the belief that the Light is the source of all creation.

The Tsardom of Moscavia is a nocturnal realm where every human was transformed into an owl-folk on a single spring night in 994, governed from the ancient capital of Moskov and guided by the Church of the Eternal Vigil.
Every human inhabitant of the Tsardom was transformed into an owl-folk on a single night in spring, an event known as the Great Changing.
Every human inhabitant of the Tsardom of Moscavia was transformed into an owl-folk on a single night in the spring of the year 994.
The Tsardom keeps a standing army of owl-folk, organized into regiments such as the White Talon and the Frosted Wing.

The Frosted Wing, a sister regiment of the standing army, draws its recruits from the commoner owl-folk and serves primarily as a cavalry force, while the White Talon remains an infantry unit devoted to close protection and urban defense.
The Tsar's standing army includes elite regiments such as the White Talon, an infantry unit drawn from noble owl-folk lineages, and the Frosted Wing, a cavalry regiment recruited from the commoners.
The Council appoints the Patriarch of Moscavia, who serves as the supreme spiritual and temporal authority of the Church and as the spiritual guarantor of the Divine Right of the Tsar.

The Patriarch is both the president of the Ecumenical Council and the supreme spiritual authority of the Church, appointed by the Council for life and serving as the living symbol of the covenant between God and Moscavia.
The supreme spiritual and temporal authority of the Church, appointed by the Ecumenical Council.

The First Codex is the oldest known written record of the art of runeweaving, containing the earliest documented principles and runic formulae of the discipline.
The First Codex is the foundational written record of the discipline, where the first runic formulae were systematically documented.
A rune can only alter a material if the weaver understands its true nature through sustained meditation.
Deepcarving is governed by the Law of Willing Stone, meaning the weaver must first understand the target material's true nature through sustained meditation before attempting the carve.
